Last week’s security disclosures offered a glimpse of the challenges ahead. Critical flaws surfaced across software that much of the internet depends on. AI agents are making vulnerabilities faster and easier to find, while the time from discovery to exploitation continues to shrink.

Companies increasingly need agents both to defend against threats and to transform how work gets done. As agents take on more responsibility, security must scale with autonomy.

Nikesh Arora, CEO of Palo Alto Networks, recently posed a question to every company adopting AI: “There are billions of dollars being spent on coding, is your coding harness secure?” For security leaders, his recommendation is clear: establish guardrails for agent deployments and deploy a second set of eyes to monitor them for drift, compliance, and verifiability.

At Replit, we’ve spent years building security into the infrastructure where agents work. When these vulnerabilities surfaced last week, that very foundation enabled us to respond quickly, effectively, and at scale . Our existing isolation protections prevented exploitation of the disclosed kernel vulnerabilities. We went further, patching affected tooling and deploying firewall protections centrally, reducing the remediation work developers would otherwise have had to do themselves.

We believe the next step is to automate more of the security response itself, with people defining the policies, approvals, and intervention points that govern the process.

As part of our Self-Driving Company blueprint , we’re bringing this infrastructure and these capabilities to other companies through Replit’s Agent Habitat. An Agent Habitat gives agents access to company knowledge and systems within boundaries the company controls, helping them delegate more work to agents without giving up control over how the work gets done.

## Security and governance for the self-driving company

Becoming self-driving requires safeguards that let companies delegate work while remaining in control. Four principles guide how we build those controls in Replit’s Agent Habitat:

• Give agents only the authority they need. Control what agents can access, which actions require approval, and how permissions carry through delegation.

• Contain failures and respond to vulnerabilities. Isolate execution, protect credentials, and respond to vulnerabilities in the environment where work happens.

• Expand access while keeping production changes accountable. Enable people to contribute while keeping production decisions subject to engineering review.

• Keep delegated work accountable and data governable. Make agent activity visible, support investigations, and establish clear boundaries for data and workloads.

Below, we take a closer look at these principles and how Replit puts them into practice.

“Our customers trust Teamworks with sensitive athlete health and performance data, so security and governance are non-negotiable. We chose Replit to help more people across our business improve our software while maintaining the security controls and engineering oversight we need.”

~ Reed Shaffner, Teamworks CTO

## 1. Give agents only the authority they need

Connecting an agent to a business system gives it authority. If a task only requires reading but the connection also permits writing, a mistake or prompt injection can have consequences beyond the task itself. Limiting access to what the work requires helps reduce that risk.

Replit’s enterprise connector management lets administrators control which groups can use each connection and define scopes for custom OAuth connectors. SAML SSO , SCIM provisioning, and role-based permissions let companies centrally manage who can build, collaborate, and ship, synchronized with their identity provider.

Credentials need a separate, stricter boundary. An agent should be able to make an authorized request without gaining access to the reusable external credential behind it. Replit keeps connector credentials outside the agent’s context. A credential broker authorizes every single request, and only retrieves the credentials from a vault and adds them to outgoing requests after that request is authorized. This reduces the risk of secrets being exposed through generated code, logs, or conversations, as well as giving finer-grained access control beyond OAuth scopes.

These controls address different risks. Permissions determine what an agent is authorized to do, while credential protection helps prevent reusable secrets from being exposed. Enterprises also need to govern how agents use the data they access, including which actions they can take with it. Together, these controls let enterprises connect agents to the systems their work requires without giving them unrestricted access to company accounts or reusable credentials.

## 2. Contain failures and respond to vulnerabilities

An agent experimenting with code should not automatically gain access to an employee’s laptop, a production database, or unrelated workloads. If an agent or the code it runs is compromised, isolation helps limit what that failure can affect.

Replit provides isolation and containment at every layer of the stack, so agents can do their best work without the risk. Based on our shared responsibility model , we are responsible for securing the harness, the runtime, and the operating system. Agents run in isolated cloud environments. MicroVMs give each execution environment its own minimal kernel, strengthening isolation between workloads. For apps using Replit’s managed databases, development and production databases are kept separate. Connector permissions provide another boundary for external systems.

This architecture mattered during this week’s Linux kernel disclosures . Replit’s existing microVM architecture with a hardened kernel configuration prevented exploitation of the Linux kernel vulnerabilities.
